name: Music streaming

naics.title: Media Streaming Distribution Services, Social Networks, and Other Media Networks and Content Providers

one_line: On-demand access to the same ~100M-song catalog, licensed from the labels. The pipe between recorded music and 900M+ paying listeners.
sells: On-demand streaming of recorded music (plus podcasts and audiobooks) through paid subscriptions and ad-supported free tiers
customers: Listeners (paid subscribers and ad-supported free users) and, on the free tiers, advertisers
suppliers: Record labels and music publishers (who license the catalog), cloud and CDN infrastructure, and device and telecom distribution partners

revenue.metric: global recorded-music streaming revenue paid through to rights holders (wholesale)
revenue.note: This is the wholesale streaming revenue paid to labels and artists (IFPI: total streaming was above $22B, 69.6% of recorded-music revenue in 2025). The streaming services collect more - subscriptions plus ads - and keep roughly 30% after paying rights holders; Spotify's own revenue was ~$17B in 2024. Subscriber shares below are MIDiA's Q4 2025 share of 921.6M global music subscribers.

structure.why: Spotify leads with ~31% of the world's 921.6M music subscribers, trailed by Tencent Music, Apple Music, YouTube Music and Amazon Music; the top five hold ~79%. No service controls the catalog, so scale and distribution - not content - decide the ranking.
structure.hhi_note: HHI from the top-5 services' subscriber shares (covering ~79% of global music subscribers). The ~21% remainder (NetEase Cloud Music, Deezer and regional services) is fragmented and adds little.

econ: Every service licenses essentially the same catalog from the same three major labels, so they cannot compete on content - they compete on price, discovery and distribution (phones, telecom bundles, hardware). Rights holders take roughly 70% of each dollar, leaving the services thin margins and a race for subscriber scale.
